topic.name: Calculating Flux in Two-Dimensional Vector Fields

question.text: Calculate the flux of the vector field $\mathbf F(x,y) = (x + y )\,\mathbf{i} + (y - x)\,\mathbf{j}$ across the closed curve $C$ given by $\mathbf r(t) = 3\cos t\,\mathbf{i} + 3\sin t\,\mathbf{j}$ for $t \in [0,2\pi).$
question.explanation:
If $\mathbf{F} = P\,\mathbf i + Q\,\mathbf j$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of $\mathbf F$ across $C$ is given by \[ \oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s = \oint\limits_{C}P\,\textrm d y - Q\,\textrm d x, \] where $\mathbf{n}$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$

Along the curve $C,$ we have \[ x = 3\cos t, \qquad y = 3\sin t. \]

Therefore,

\begin{align*} P(x,y) &= x + y = 3(\cos t + \sin t), \\[7pt] Q(x,y) &= y - x = 3(\sin t - \cos t ). \end{align*}

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

\begin{align*} \dfrac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} &= \dfrac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3\cos t) = -3\sin t, \\[10pt] \dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} &= \dfrac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3\sin t) = 3\cos t. \end{align*}

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

\begin{align*} \oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s &= \oint\limits_C P \: \text{d}y - Q \: \text{d}x \\[5pt] &= \int_0^{2\pi} \left(P \cdot \dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} - Q \cdot \dfrac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} \right) \textrm{d}t \\[5pt] &= \int_0^{2\pi} \big( 3(\cos t + \sin t) \big) \cdot \big( 3\cos t \big) - \big(3(\sin t - \cos t )\big) \cdot \big( -3\sin t\big) \: \textrm{d}t \\[5pt] &= 9 \int_0^{2\pi} (\cos^2 t + \sin t \cos t +\sin^2 t-\sin t \cos t )\: \textrm{d}t \\[5pt] &= 9 \int_0^{2\pi} 1 \: \textrm{d}t \\[5pt] &= 9t \Bigg|_0^{2\pi} \\[5pt] &= 9(2\pi-0)\\[5pt] &= 18 \pi \end{align*}

question.text: Calculate the flux of the vector field $\mathbf F(x,y) = xy\,\mathbf{i} + x^2\,\mathbf{j}$ across the closed curve $C$ given by $\mathbf r(t) = 2\cos t\,\mathbf{i} + 2\sin t\,\mathbf{j}$ for $t \in [0,2\pi).$
question.explanation:
If $\mathbf{F} = P\,\mathbf i + Q\,\mathbf j$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of $\mathbf F$ across $C$ is given by \[ \oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s = \oint\limits_{C}P\,\textrm d y - Q\,\textrm d x, \] where $\mathbf{n}$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$

Along the curve $C,$ we have \[ x = 2\cos t, \qquad y = 2\sin t. \]

Therefore,

\begin{align*} P(x,y) &= xy = 4\sin t \cos t, \\[7pt] Q(x,y) &= x^2 =4\cos^2 t. \end{align*}

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

\begin{align*} \dfrac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} &= \dfrac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\cos t) = -2\sin t, \\[10pt] \dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} &= \dfrac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\sin t) = 2\cos t. \end{align*}

Finally, we evaluate the integral using the substitution $u=\cos t, \textrm d u = -\sin t \,\textrm d t,$ as follows:

\begin{align*} \oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s &= \oint\limits_C P \: \text{d}y - Q \: \text{d}x \\[5pt] &= \int_0^{2\pi} \left(P \cdot \dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} - Q \cdot \dfrac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} \right) \textrm{d}t \\[5pt] &= \int_0^{2\pi} \big( 4\sin t \cos t \big) \cdot \big( 2\cos t \big) - \big(4\cos^2 t \big) \cdot \big( -2\sin t \big) \: \textrm{d}t \\[5pt] &= \int_0^{2\pi} 8 \sin t \cos^2 t + 8 \sin t \cos^2 t \: \textrm{d}t \\[5pt] &= \int_0^{2\pi} 16 \sin t \cos^2 t \: \textrm{d}t \\[5pt] &= \int_1^{1} -16 u^2 \: \textrm{d}u \\[5pt] &= 0 \end{align*}

example.title: Calculating the Flux of a Vector Field Over a Closed Curve in Parametric Form

question.text: Calculate the flux of the vector field $\mathbf F(x,y) = e^y\,\mathbf{i} + e^x\,\mathbf{j}$ across the closed curve $C$ given by $\mathbf r(t) = 3\cos t\,\mathbf{i} + 4\sin t\,\mathbf{j}$ for $t \in [0,2\pi).$
question.explanation:
If $\mathbf{F} = P\,\mathbf i + Q\,\mathbf j$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of $\mathbf F$ across $C$ is given by \[ \oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s = \oint\limits_{C}P\,\textrm d y - Q\,\textrm d x, \] where $\mathbf{n}$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$

Along the curve $C,$ we have \[ x = 3\cos t, \qquad y = 4\sin t. \]

Therefore,

\begin{align*} P(x,y) &= e^y = e^{4\sin t}, \\[7pt] Q(x,y) &= e^x = e^{3\cos t}. \end{align*}

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

\begin{align*} \dfrac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} &= \dfrac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3\cos t) = -3\sin t, \\[10pt] \dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} &= \dfrac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4\sin t) = 4\cos t. \end{align*}

Finally, we evaluate the integral using the substitutions $u = 4\sin t, \mathrm du = 4\cos t\,\mathrm d t$ and $v = 3\cos t, \mathrm d v = -3\sin t\,\mathrm d t,$ as follows:

\begin{align*} \oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s &= \oint\limits_C P \: \text{d}y - Q \: \text{d}x \\[5pt] &= \int_0^{2\pi} \left(P \cdot \dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} - Q \cdot \dfrac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} \right) \textrm{d}t \\[5pt] &= \int_0^{2\pi} \big( e^{4\sin t} \big) \cdot \big( 4\cos t \big) - \big( e^{3\cos t} \big) \cdot \big( -3\sin t \big) \: \textrm{d}t \\[5pt] &= \int_0^{2\pi} \big( e^{4\sin t} \big) \cdot \big( 4\cos t \big) \: \textrm{d}t- \int_0^{2\pi}\big( e^{3\cos t} \big) \cdot \big( -3\sin t \big) \: \textrm{d}t \\[5pt] &= \int_0^{0} e^u \:\mathrm d u - \int_1^1 e^{v} \: \textrm{d}v \\[5pt] &= 0 \end{align*}

example.title: Calculating the Flux of a Vector Field Over a Closed Curve in Parametric Form

question.text: Calculate the flux of the vector field $\mathbf F(x,y) = y\,\mathbf{i} + 9x^3\,\mathbf{j}$ across the closed curve $C$ given by $\mathbf r(t) = \cos t\,\mathbf{i} + 3\sin t\,\mathbf{j}$ for $t \in [0,2\pi).$
question.explanation:
If $\mathbf{F} = P\,\mathbf i + Q\,\mathbf j$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of $\mathbf F$ across $C$ is given by \[ \oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s = \oint\limits_{C}P\,\textrm d y - Q\,\textrm d x, \] where $\mathbf{n}$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$

Along the curve $C,$ we have \[ x = \cos t, \qquad y = 3\sin t. \]

Therefore,

\begin{align*} P(x,y) &= y = 3\sin t, \\[5pt] Q(x,y) &= 9x^3 = 9\cos^3 t. \end{align*}

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

\begin{align*} \dfrac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} &= \dfrac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\cos t) = -\sin t, \\[10pt] \dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} &= \dfrac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3\sin t) = 3\cos t. \end{align*}

Finally, we evaluate the integral using the substitution $\cos t = u, \mathrm d u = -\sin t \,\mathrm d t,$ as follows:

\begin{align*} \oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s &= \oint\limits_C P \: \text{d}y - Q \: \text{d}x \\[5pt] &= \int_0^{2\pi} \left(P \cdot \dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} - Q \cdot \dfrac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} \right) \textrm{d}t \\[5pt] &= \int_0^{2\pi} \big( 3\sin t \big) \cdot \big( 3\cos t \big) - \big(9\cos^3 t\big) \cdot \big( -\sin t\big) \: \textrm{d}t \\[5pt] &= 9 \int_0^{2\pi} (\sin t \cos t +\sin t \cos^3 t)\: \textrm{d}t \\[5pt] &= -9 \int_1^{1} (u +u^3)\: \textrm{d}u \\[5pt] &= 0 \end{align*}

example.title: Calculating the Flux of a Vector Field Over a Closed Curve in Parametric Form

question.text: Calculate the flux of the vector field $\mathbf F(x,y) =4x\,\mathbf{i} + 4y\,\mathbf{j}$ across the closed curve $C$ given by $\mathbf r(t) = 8\cos t\,\mathbf{i} + 6\sin t\,\mathbf{j}$ for $t \in [0,2\pi).$
question.explanation:
If $\mathbf{F} = P\,\mathbf i + Q\,\mathbf j$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of $\mathbf F$ across $C$ is given by \[ \oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s = \oint\limits_{C}P\,\textrm d y - Q\,\textrm d x, \] where $\mathbf{n}$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$

Along the curve $C,$ we have \[ x = 8\cos t, \qquad y = 6\sin t. \]

Therefore,

\begin{align*} P(x,y) &= 4x = 4(8\cos t) = 32\cos t, \\[7pt] Q(x,y) &= 4y = 4(6\sin t) = 24\sin t. \end{align*}

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

\begin{align*} \dfrac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} &= \dfrac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(8\cos t) = -8\sin t, \\[10pt] \dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} &= \dfrac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(6\sin t) = 6\cos t. \end{align*}

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

\begin{align*} \oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s &= \oint\limits_C P \: \text{d}y - Q \: \text{d}x \\[5pt] &= \int_0^{2\pi} \left(P \cdot \dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} - Q \cdot \dfrac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} \right) \textrm{d}t \\[5pt] &= \int_0^{2\pi} \left( 32\cos t \right)\cdot \big( 6\cos t \big) - \left( 24\sin t \right) \cdot \big( -8 \sin t \big) \: \textrm{d}t \\[5pt] &= \int_0^{2\pi} 192(\cos^2t + \sin^2 t) \: \textrm{d}t \\[5pt] &= \int_0^{2\pi} 192 \: \textrm{d}t \\[5pt] &= 192t \Bigg|_0^{2\pi} \\[5pt] &= 192(2\pi-0) \\[5pt] &= 384\pi \end{align*}
